title: Fed Holds 10-2 With Two Votes to Hike, as Healey's Boring Budget Calms Gilts and Brent Settles at $115
subhead: The FOMC left the funds rate at 3.75-4% but two dissents pushed December hike odds to about 82%, while UK Chancellor John Healey delivered a deficit-neutral budget that drew a 5bp outperformance of gilts over Treasuries and Brent settled up 1% at $115.32 ahead of Thursday's ECB decision.

sections.heading: The Fed Holds, and Two Voters Say That Isn't Enough
sections.body:
The FOMC voted 10-2 on Wednesday to keep the federal funds target at 3.75% to 4%, following the 25-basis-point hike in September that was the first increase since July 2023, according to Fox Business coverage of the decision. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Governor Lisa Cook both dissented in favor of an immediate quarter-point hike. The statement upgraded the description of activity to expanding at a strong pace and repeated that inflation remains elevated.

Chair Kevin Warsh used the press conference to rule out a soft target: 'there's no soft inflation target and no implicit inflation target,' he said, adding that inflation has run above the committee's objective for close to six years. He also said he does not believe in forward guidance outside a crisis and announced that from 2027 one FOMC meeting a year will be dedicated to strategy with no rate vote or statement. Warsh said politics played no role in the decision despite it landing six days before the midterms, and flagged that oil futures have moved up over recent weeks.

Pricing moved accordingly. Per FXStreet, traders pushed the odds of a December hike to about 81% from roughly 75%, and CME FedWatch as cited by Fox Business showed 82.6% for a December increase, up from 78.3% a day earlier. Goldman Sachs Asset Management's Kay Haigh told Fox Business the firm expects the Fed to 'resume rate hikes in December.'
sections.whyItMatters: Cook's first dissent since joining in 2022, alongside a hawk from Cleveland, makes the hold look like a pause rather than a plateau. With a December hike now the base case, the cost of dollar funding stays elevated into year-end and the Fed is effectively anchoring policy to an oil price it does not control.

sections.heading: Healey's Budget Is Deliberately Dull, and That Is the Point
sections.body:
New UK Chancellor John Healey delivered his first Budget on Wednesday and kept to the fiscal path inherited from Rachel Reeves, holding roughly £15bn of headroom and targeting net debt below 83% of GDP, according to Portfolio Adviser. The political content was real: the bank surcharge doubled to 6%, a one-off £100 payment to 20 million households to offset energy bills, a First-Time Buyer ISA replacing the Lifetime ISA, and an adjusted triple lock paired with a new national care service that Healey said would save £15bn a year by the late 2030s and £50bn by 2050, per Reuters coverage via Yahoo/Euronews.

Healey cut the 2027 growth forecast to 1.0% from the 1.6% Labour projected in early March, while lifting 2026 to 1.2% from 1.1%.

The market verdict was relief, not enthusiasm. Gilts outperformed US Treasuries by about 5 basis points during the session, with the 10-year yield near 5.31% at 2pm London time — only around 20bp below October's peak, which was the highest since 2007, per Guinness Global Dynamic Bond's Craig Veysey. Schroders' James Bilson called it 'uneventful — and this is exactly what the bond market wanted to see.' Reuters reported Britain will issue an extra £4.4 billion of gilts and cut longer-dated sales, a mix analysts at Rathbones said should support the long end by reducing duration supply.
sections.whyItMatters: The UK's problem was never the size of a single giveaway, it was credibility with the long end. A budget that raises bank taxes to fund household energy relief — while financing it from within existing rules — buys the gilt market time at 5.3%. The real event is now the December remit: heavier bill issuance and less long paper is the only thing standing between the 10-year and a retest of 2007 highs.

sections.heading: Brent Settles $115.32 on a Saudi Refinery Hit and a Midterm Strike Option
sections.body:
Brent rose $1.44, or 1%, to settle at $115.32 and WTI jumped 3% to $102.78, per Reuters' Scott DiSavino. Three things moved it: the Houthis said on Tuesday they had struck Saudi Arabia's largest refinery — a 550,000 barrel-per-day facility that Saudi authorities had not immediately confirmed — and hit Aden airport on Wednesday; analysts including BOK Financial's Dennis Kissler expect renewed US military operations against Iran after the November 3 midterms; and the EIA reported a surprise 1.9 million barrel draw in crude stocks against a forecast 15,000 barrel build.

The diplomatic track is not dead but is not working. Qatari mediators presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the eight-month war; a senior Iranian official told Reuters the draft contained 'only unacceptable ideas' that did not amount to an offer, while Iran's foreign minister said Tehran continues to give diplomacy a chance.

On the supply side, traders told Reuters Russian crude exports from Baltic and Black Sea ports could fall next month as domestic refiners lift diesel output under this month's deal with Washington, and China issued a rare fourth batch of fuel export quotas. OPEC+ meets Sunday with December targets expected to stay unchanged.
sections.whyItMatters: Brent has been overbought four times in five sessions on the same forward-looking fear rather than an actual barrel loss. The market is now pricing a post-election escalation as roughly certain, which means the risk is asymmetric: a strike that arrives is already in the price, while a Qatar-brokered ceasefire — which Iran has publicly not accepted — is the under-priced shock.

sections.heading: The Euro Meets the ECB at Its October Floor
sections.body:
EUR/USD closed Wednesday just above 1.1100, a level it has now touched twice this month after five straight losing sessions, per FXStreet, which put the pair back near 1.1150 ahead of Thursday's decision. The ECB's deposit rate is forecast to stay at 2.5%, with Lagarde's press conference at 13:45 GMT.

The rate gap is doing the work. US third-quarter GDP lands Thursday at 12:30 GMT with forecasts around 3.2% annualized after 2.2%, while euro-area third-quarter growth on Friday is forecast at 0.2% after 0.6%. Reuters' Open Interest column noted the ECB could make a case for markets to dial back bets on another hike this week, but 'whether it wants to do so is another matter.'

The euro also has a fiscal drag behind it. Euro-zone yields moved higher on Wednesday as French sovereign debt resumed falling in price after the brief Moody's relief rally, according to Dow Jones reporting via Yahoo Finance, which said German bunds followed.
sections.whyItMatters: The ECB has to defend 1.11 with a hold while US growth accelerates and the Fed leans hawkish — a combination that argues for further downside. The more interesting question is whether Lagarde acknowledges that energy-driven inflation from the Gulf gives her cover to stay neutral, which would quietly remove the euro's only rate-differential support.

sections.heading: Beijing Fights Its Own AI Bubble
sections.body:
China's STAR 50 index of AI and chip companies has fallen about 40% from its July high, erasing roughly $480 billion in market value in four months, according to Reuters data cited by several outlets. The FT reported Beijing is now rushing to shore up markets as the AI trade reverses amid slowing growth. Goldman Sachs estimates AI stocks account for 42% of China's market value and 57% of trading, per Reuters figures cited by 24/7 Wall St. The index's price-to-earnings ratio peaked near 250 and still sits around 100, against roughly 30 for the Nasdaq 100.

Individual names are worse: Unitree has lost about half its value since its August debut, GPU makers MetaX and Moore Threads roughly halved since July, and optical suppliers Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink are about 60% below summer highs, per the same reporting. Morgan Stanley expects offshore Chinese equities to fall another 10-15% before bottoming.

The offshore channel has been brutal for foreign holders — the KraneShares STAR 50 ETF (KSTR) fell 42.63% from the June 30 close through midday Wednesday and is flat for the year, wiping out the entire summer rally.
sections.whyItMatters: State-backed buyers reportedly sold into the rally to cool the boom, then stepped in to support the selloff — a managed deflation that is now the Chinese market's operating principle. For global allocators the lesson is about concentration: a theme at 57% of turnover turns a sector correction into a national market event, and that template is being watched in New York.

sections.heading: Washington Sanctions a Friendly Government's Military
sections.body:
The US imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defense ministry on Wednesday over Kigali's involvement in mineral-rich eastern Congo, where fighting continues between Congolese forces and Rwandan-backed rebels despite peace efforts, according to ABC News/Reuters. The move escalates a sanctions campaign that began in March, when Treasury's OFAC designated the Rwanda Defence Force and senior commanders over support for the M23 armed group.

Separately, Treasury announced fresh North Korea-related designations targeting an IT-worker scheme involving North Korean and Russian nationals, per NBC News and Treasury coverage — the financial-crime variant of sanctions that targets revenue channels rather than weapons programs.
sections.whyItMatters: Sanctioning the army of a government Washington has been courting on migration and minerals is a significant escalation in the conflict-minerals space, and it puts banks and refiners handling eastern Congolese gold, coltan and tin on notice. That is where the compliance risk actually lands, not on the ministry itself.

sections.heading: Mexico Races the Midterms for a Tariff Deal
sections.body:
President Claudia Sheinbaum said Wednesday that trade talks with Washington are advancing and both sides are assessing whether an interim deal can be reached before the November 3 midterms, per Reuters. Mexico is seeking a significant reduction in US tariffs on autos, steel and aluminum, and the agreement would address US concerns over automotive content and Chinese investment.

The context is USMCA in limbo: Washington declined in July to extend the pact for another 16 years, pushing it into annual reviews, and US-Canada talks collapsed last month into a tariff fight including US import bans on Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and dairy, with Ottawa vowing dollar-for-dollar retaliation.
sections.whyItMatters: Mexico is betting that cooperation gets tariff relief faster than confrontation — a live test of whether the USMCA dispute channel still functions for a partner that stays at the table. Anything signed this week becomes the template for how Washington handles content rules and Chinese capital in North American supply chains.

bottomLine: Wednesday was a day of institutions deciding not to move and markets pricing the next move anyway. The Fed held at 3.75-4% with two dissents and December hike odds near 82%, which tells you the committee's next step is up barring an oil collapse. Healey's deliberately dull UK budget bought gilts a 5bp edge over Treasuries and left the 10-year at 5.31%, with the December remit now the real fiscal event. Brent settled at $115.32 with a post-midterm strike on Iran already embedded, which makes a Qatar-brokered ceasefire the under-priced risk rather than an escalation. Thursday brings the ECB at 2.5% with EUR/USD pinned at its October floor, US Q3 GDP forecast at 3.2%, and the widening transatlantic rate gap that follows from it.
sources: Fox Business, Reuters, FXStreet, Portfolio Adviser, Schroders, Guinness Global Dynamic Bond, Rathbones, Yahoo Finance/Euronews, Dow Jones Newswires, Financial Times, 24/7 Wall St., Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, ABC News, NBC News, US Treasury OFAC, SunSirs, CME FedWatch
